k892: Apartments, houses, commercial space — all open to foreign buyers on identical terms to citizens, no reciprocity requirement, no special permit. The single exception is agricultural land, or <s1>truall bujqësor</s1>: direct purchase is barred for foreign individuals. The two ways around it are an Albanian <s3>sh.p.k.</s3> company, which can hold agricultural land the way a foreign individual can't, or a lease running up to 99 years, which functions as ownership for most practical purposes without transferring the title itself. Neither route matters to the large majority of buyers, since almost nobody is buying farmland — but it's worth knowing the boundary exists before a listing surprises you with it.
k893: Inheritance carries through the same equal-terms rule: a foreign owner's heirs inherit Albanian property exactly as an Albanian citizen's would.
k894: How you actually pay for it
k895: This is the part the "yes, foreigners can buy" headline skips. A non-resident mortgage from an Albanian bank is close to unobtainable in practice — the market simply isn't built around lending to buyers without local income or a long banking relationship. What fills the gap instead is developer financing: 0% instalments running from reservation to key handover is the standard closing instrument on new-build sales, not a special favour. Buyers who need financing structure their purchase around this rather than a mortgage, and most buyers who can pay cash do, since it's also the fastest route through the process — SWIFT transfer straight to the notary's escrow account, no local account required to complete a purchase (though opening one is possible, if slow, for buyers who want one afterward).
k896: What foreign buyers are actually afraid of
k901: An independent lawyer pulling the ASHK extract yourself — "no extract, no money transfer" is the working rule
k903: Buying finished stock with the hipotekë already cleared, or checking the developer's track record before paying anything
k905: An independent engineer's inspection, not the developer's own sign-off
k907: One transparent contract, bank transfer only, full price stated
k909: An honest financial model, and a zone with a real off-season economy, not just a summer one
k911: Prevention through the four items above — "I'll just sue" is a losing plan given how long it takes
k912: This list is ranked by how often it comes up across DomLivo's review of foreign-buyer forums, agency interviews and documented complaints — not a generic worry list, an actual frequency ranking.
k914: Foreign buyers aren't one group with one set of concerns — Polish and Czech buyers cluster on the coast chasing short-term-rental returns, Italians buy in Vlorë for climate and ferry links as much as investment, and German and Swiss buyers lean on lawyer-intermediary channels rather than direct agency deals. <s1>A fuller breakdown of who's buying, from where, and why</s1> is worth reading if you're trying to gauge how competitive a given zone actually is.
k915: That range runs all the way up from a single apartment to institutional scale — Eagle Hills, Adal Holdings and Kushner-linked entities are all foreign investors too, just operating multi-hundred-million-euro developments rather than buying one flat. There's no dedicated REIT or fund market to speak of, since Albania has no real stock exchange for one to list on, so almost all of that institutional money arrives as direct project investment rather than through a fund a smaller foreign buyer could also put money into.
k916: Where it's gone wrong for real buyers
k917: A Finnish buyer who paid for an off-plan unit in Sarandë never received the keys; the story is documented well enough that a memorial site now exists cataloguing it, and <s1>the buyer's own conclusion, reported afterward, was blunt</s1>: only buy finished stock with the <s3>hipotekë</s3> already registered, never off-plan on a promise.
k918: A Tirana buyer who prepaid 40% notarially in 2008 still had no keys three years later — a reminder that "notarial" alone doesn't mean "protected" if the underlying project stalls.
k919: <s0>Another documented case</s0>: a €20,000 "reservation" paid under agent pressure, construction then stopped, and the contract had no refund clause at all. The pattern across all three is the same — money moved before the protections that would have caught the problem were actually checked.
k920: The one document that matters most
k921: Every fear on the list above traces back to the same document: the <s1>kartela e pasurisë</s1>, the ownership extract from ASHK. Pull it yourself, independently, before any money moves — not the version a seller or agent hands you. <s3>The eight things that specifically go wrong on Albanian titles are covered in full separately</s3>, but the rule that matters here is simpler than the list: if you can't get a clean extract, that is the answer, not a problem to solve after paying a deposit. Once the legal picture is clear, <s5>what's actually on the market</s5> is the next real question.

k939: If you are weighing an apartment in Durrës Yachts & Marina, the short answer from our research is: not until the foundation question is settled. Two of the three built towers have been confirmed to be sinking, the project is financed mostly by buyers' own deposits, and the port it is meant to replace is still working where it has always been. None of that means the project will fail. It means the risk sits with the buyer, and the price does not reflect it.
k941: The marina is Albania's largest property development: a joint venture in which Eagle Hills and Nshmi hold 67% and the state agency ASDC holds 33%, with the state contributing the land and an exemption from the infrastructure tax. The plan is about 13,000 apartments — 93% of the floor area is housing — plus 280 yacht berths, at a declared €2–2.5 billion. So far three towers have been built, out of roughly 1,680 apartments in the first phase.
k942: What has gone wrong so far
k943: In May 2026 the construction inspectorate IKMT confirmed that two of the built towers have settled, by 28 cm and 18 cm. A subcontractor claims the movement is as much as 74 cm; we could not verify that figure. The problem reported is that the piles were not driven to suit the sandy ground — the same soil that runs along the whole Durrës coast.
k944: The money is the second issue. The investor's own funds cover about 6.8% of the project; the rest relies mainly on pre-sales. Those raised about €42 million in 2023–24 against a company capital of €7 million, and the investor's plan projects a 615% return. Sales also began before the permits were in place, and the European Commission has been following the deal.
k946: The marina is built on the idea that the cargo port moves out of the city to Porto Romano, a €400–410 million project. The tender for it has failed twice; in March 2026 the only bidder, Archirodon, did not submit an offer. The government says the move will go ahead. Until it does, the whole timeline of the marina — and the view many buyers are paying for — depends on a port that has no contractor.
k948: Launch prices were €1,500–1,600/m². Asking prices are now €2,000–3,000/m², €4,000–5,500/m² with a view of the marina, and penthouses go up to €1.2 million. k949: How to check before you pay anything
k950: The checks are the same for any off-plan purchase in Albania; here they simply matter more.
k951: Look the company up in the business register QKB: owners, capital, status and beneficial owners.
k952: Pull the ownership certificate for the plot and any mortgages from the cadastre ASHK yourself, not from the sales office.
k953: Ask for the building permit (leje ndërtimi) for your tower, and remember that a finished building also needs an occupancy permit (leje përdorimi).
k954: Pay no more than a 5–10% deposit before those checks are done.
k955: Sign the reservation contract (kontrata e porosisë) in notarial form and register it — a contract for a unit under construction can be registered under instruction no. 1557 of 18.09.2024 — and ask for payments to go through an account blocked at the notary.
k956: Compare the number of floors built with the number in the permit.
k958: In our 2026 assessment the marina is on the list of ideas we would avoid until the foundation problem is resolved: pre-sales without escrow, sandy ground and a dependence on a port move that has not started is the highest concentration of risk in the country. If you want a new apartment by the sea in Durrës now, a finished building with its occupancy permit carries none of these three risks.
